ties.citation: Borland International (1985). TURBO Pascal Reference Manual, Version 3.0. Introduction, section "TURBO Pascal".
ties.quote: TURBO Pascal closely follows the definition of Standard Pascal as defined by K. Jensen and N. Wirth in the Pascal User Manual and Report. The few and minor differences are described in Appendix D.
ties.what: the whole language: Standard Pascal (Jensen and Wirth) with extensions
ties.reason: Official manual states the language follows Standard Pascal. Read from the OCR text layer of the scanned manual (bitsavers mirror); the OCR renders 'Report' as 'Re po ri', corrected here. Appendix D of the same manual repeats it: "The TURBO Pascal language follows the Standard Pascal defined by Jensen and Wirth in their User Manual and Report, with only minor differences introduced for the sheer purpose of efficiency." The same introduction names Wirth as the designer of Pascal.

ties.citation: Civeyrac, A.-L. (2019). The One Who Created Languages (interview with Anders Hejlsberg). Welcome to the Jungle, 11 February 2019.
ties.quote: Delphi, in many ways, was really just sort of a successor to Turbo Pascal.
ties.what: the language and compiler line: Delphi's Object Pascal continues Turbo/Borland Pascal
ties.reason: Designer's own words, but 'successor' is product-lineage wording and does not itself say what was taken; hence 'partly'. A human should decide whether this counts as design (strong) or product lineage (weak under the rule). The quote was returned by the fetch tool's reader, not seen in raw page text, hence medium confidence.

alternatives.citation: Intersimone, D. (2026). Delphi and Turbo Pascal - 43 Years of Continuous Innovation. Embarcadero blog, 10 February 2026.
alternatives.quote: Following version 7.0, Borland ceased the Turbo Pascal line to focus on its successor, Delphi, which launched on February 14, 1995, transitioning the language into a full Rapid Application Development (RAD) environment for Windows.
alternatives.comment: Vendor (Embarcadero, owner of Delphi) blog by a long-time Borland employee. Also product-lineage wording, though 'transitioning the language' treats it as one language.

alternatives.citation: Cantu, M. (1995-2020). Essential Pascal, 4th edition, chapter 1 "A Short History of the Pascal Language", section "Delphi's Pascal".
alternatives.quote: After 9 versions of Turbo and Borland Pascal compilers, which gradually extended the language, Borland released Delphi in 1995, turning Pascal into a visual programming language.
alternatives.comment: This is the source of the current Pascal -> Delphi quote. It is a secondary source (book author, not the designer or vendor at the time of writing) and it supports Turbo Pascal -> Delphi better than Pascal -> Delphi, because it says the Turbo and Borland Pascal compilers extended the language before Delphi. Next sentence: "Delphi extends the Pascal language in a number of ways, including many object-oriented extensions which are different from other flavors of Object Pascal, including those in the Borland Pascal with Objects compiler."

ties.citation: Borland International (1989). Turbo Pascal 5.5 Object-Oriented Programming Guide. Introduction, p. 1.
ties.quote: The object-oriented extensions in Turbo Pascal 5.5 were inspired by Larry Tesler's "Object Pascal Report" (Apple, 1985) and Bjarne Stroustrup's "The C++ Programming Language" (1986, Addison-Wesley).
ties.what: object-oriented extensions (objects, inheritance, virtual methods, constructors and destructors)
ties.reason: Official manual names Stroustrup's C++ book as one of two inspirations for the 5.5 object extensions; the other is Apple's Object Pascal (off-map). A later-version, single-feature-area influence, so weak; could be argued strong because objects define later Turbo Pascal and Delphi. Read from the PDF text layer. Chapter 1 (p. 8) adds: "In its object philosophy, Turbo Pascal 5.5 is more like C++ than Smalltalk."

ties.citation: Borland International (1989). Turbo Pascal 5.5 Object-Oriented Programming Guide. Chapter 1, p. 8.
ties.quote: In its object philosophy, Turbo Pascal 5.5 is more like C++ than Smalltalk. Smalltalk is an interpreter, while from the beginning, Turbo Pascal has been a pure native code compiler.
ties.reason: Not a tie. The manual names Smalltalk only to say Turbo Pascal is unlike it.

ties.citation: Borland International (1989). Turbo Pascal 5.5 Object-Oriented Programming Guide. Chapter 1, p. 23.
ties.reason: Not a tie. Simula-67 is mentioned once, as the first object-oriented language, created for writing simulations; no statement that Turbo Pascal took anything from it. No clean sentence recorded (OCR line breaks).

No primary statement found. Checked: Borland's Turbo Pascal 4.0 press release of 9 September 1987 (https://discmaster.textfiles.com/view/1969/RBBSIABOX31.cdr/trac/tp4.rls) describes units and separate compilation without naming Modula-2 or UCSD Pascal; the 3.0 manual and the 5.5 OOP Guide do not mention Modula-2. The 4.0 Owner's Handbook PDF (bitsavers mirror) was too large to fetch and was not read. Wikipedia (secondary) says units were adopted from UCSD Pascal (off-map) and only that the system was 'similar to' Modula-2. Do not add.

ties.citation: Winer, E. (1987). Interview with Greg Whitten. QuickTALK, vol. 1, no. 1.
ties.quote: The first version of this compiler was fairly limited, really just a slight superset of BASICA. [...] When we created IBM BASCOM 2.0 we added subprograms, some new graphics support, and we added large arrays. From that product we produced QuickBASIC 1.0, which is essentially a compiler without an environment.
ties.what: the whole language: QuickBASIC 1.0 was produced from Microsoft's BASIC compiler (BASCOM), itself a superset of BASICA (the Microsoft-written interpreted BASIC for the IBM PC)
ties.reason: Whitten was Microsoft's Director of Languages R&D and co-wrote the BASCOM compiler. The two parts come from two consecutive answers (joined with [...]): 'this compiler' is BASCOM 1.0, and 'that product' is IBM BASCOM 2.0. The source names BASICA, not Dartmouth BASIC, so the tie to the map's generic 'basic' node is by dialect; hence 'partly'. The page is a fan-site transcription of the 1987 newsletter; sentences were returned by the fetch tool's reader and were identical across two fetches. Supporting, from Microsoft's manual Programming in BASIC (QuickBASIC 4.5, 1988; https://www.pcjs.org/documents/books/mspl13/basic/qbprog): "The term "BASICA" refers to interpreted versions of BASIC in general." and the manual explains block IF and DO...LOOP to readers 'coming to this version of BASIC after programming in BASICA' (partial wording only).

ties.citation: Microsoft Corporation (1991). Microsoft Visual Basic. Microsoft News Releases, document Q72316 PR, May 1991 (updated 23 May 1991).
ties.quote: The Visual Basic language is a powerful, structured, general-purpose programming language. It is a derivative of the Microsoft QuickBasic(TM) modern programming system.
ties.what: the BASIC language of Visual Basic (Subs and Functions, block If, Select Case, Do loops, error trapping) and the threaded p-code incremental compiler
ties.reason: Microsoft-side statement from the Visual Basic 1.0 launch backgrounder, a good second source next to Alan Cooper's essay. The same document says the threaded p-code incremental compiler is 'a technology first introduced in Microsoft QuickBasic programming system version 4.0 in 1987' (fragments only, not a full verbatim sentence). The copy is a text file (VBFACTS.TXT) preserved on a shareware CD; sentences were returned by the fetch tool's reader and were identical across two fetches.

ties.what: structured constructs (block IF, SELECT CASE, DO loops, procedures, records)
ties.reason: No primary statement found. In the 1987 QuickTALK interview Whitten attributes the new control structures to the ANSI BASIC standard, not to Pascal: "We extended the control structures, for example adding Select/Case and Do statements, which are ANSI constructs." He mentions FORTRAN and Pascal only as a contrast in runtime behavior. The QuickBASIC 4.5 manual (first 100,000 characters read) mentions C and Pascal once, in a comparison of NOT operators. Do not add. The same holds for C and ALGOL.

ties.citation: Morris, R. (2009). Anders Hejlsberg: Geek of the Week. Simple Talk (Redgate), 19 March 2009.
ties.quote: Java was one of them, but C++ and Delphi also influenced our design.
ties.reason: Not found for Turbo Pascal. Hejlsberg names Delphi (and Java and C++) as influences on C#, not Turbo Pascal, so this quote supports Delphi -> C# (and Java -> C#, C++ -> C#), not Turbo Pascal -> C#. The Artima interview 'The C# Design Process' mentions Turbo Pascal and Delphi only as earlier projects he designed. The Computerworld A-Z interview on C# was unreachable.

No Microsoft statement found that ties VBA directly to QuickBASIC (one search, no primary hit). Sources describe VBA as coming from Visual Basic; the route from QuickBASIC is through Visual Basic. Do not add.

turbopascal.first_version: Turbo Pascal 1.0, 20 November 1983 (CP/M, CP/M-86 and MS-DOS)
turbopascal.designer_note: Hejlsberg wrote the compiler core in Denmark at his company PolyData (Blue Label Pascal for the Nascom, 1981; then Compas Pascal / PolyPascal); Borland licensed it and added the editor and user interface. Hejlsberg (Artima, 2003): "I designed Turbo Pascal mostly by myself."
turbopascal.country: Denmark (compiler core); United States (Borland, Scotts Valley, California)
turbopascal.last_version: Turbo Pascal 7.0 / Borland Pascal 7.0, 27 October 1992 (7.01 was the only bugfix release)
famous_software: ZZT (Tim Sweeney, 1991): per Wikipedia, citing Sweeney's 2009 Gamasutra interview, he first developed it in Turbo Pascal
MicroCalc: the demonstration spreadsheet shipped on the Turbo Pascal disk
turbopascal.status: Discontinued after version 7 (1992) in favor of Delphi. Borland later released versions 1.0, 3.02 and 5.5 as freeware. Free Pascal maintains a Turbo Pascal compatibility mode ({$mode TP}, option -Mtp) that mimics Turbo Pascal 7, and Delphi still compiles much Turbo Pascal code.

quickbasic.first_version: QuickBASIC 1.0, 18 August 1985 (a compiler without an environment; the editor came with 2.0)
quickbasic.designer_note: No single designer is documented. Greg Whitten (Director of Languages R&D at Microsoft in 1987) co-wrote the BASCOM compiler that QuickBASIC 1.0 came from, and said of the QuickBASIC 4 team: "If you count me, there are nine of us." and that he was not the project leader. A secondary history (George Mack, 2002) says Tom Button headed the team; not checked against a primary source.
quickbasic.last_version: QuickBASIC 4.5 (1988); continued as BASIC Professional Development System 7.1 (QuickBASIC Extended, October 1990). QBasic 1.0 (1991, shipped with MS-DOS 5) is an interpreter-only subset of QuickBASIC 4.5; QBasic 1.1 (1993) was its last version.
famous_software: Gorillas (QBasic sample game shipped with MS-DOS 5, 1991)
Nibbles (QBasic sample game shipped with MS-DOS 5, 1991)
quickbasic.famous_software_note: Both are QBasic programs by Microsoft, not QuickBASIC compiler programs. No reliably documented well-known program written in QuickBASIC proper was found.
quickbasic.status: Discontinued; Microsoft's successor was Visual Basic (including Visual Basic 1.0 for MS-DOS, 1992). Independent compatible successors, per Wikipedia: QB64 (a QuickBASIC-to-C++ translator for Windows, Linux and macOS) and FreeBASIC (partial compatibility). Whether QB64 is currently maintained was not checked.

notes: Method: WebSearch and WebFetch only. Three quotes were read directly from the text layer of PDFs saved by WebFetch (Turbo Pascal 3.0 manual, 5.5 OOP Guide): confidence high. Quotes from HTML or text pages came through the fetch tool's reader, which returns sentences in short segments; they are marked medium, and the two most important (Whitten, Microsoft Q72316) were identical across two fetches. Off-map influences stated by primary sources: Apple's Object Pascal (Tesler's 'Object Pascal Report', 1985) on Turbo Pascal 5.5 objects; ANSI BASIC constructs (Select/Case, Do) on QuickBASIC 4; Microsoft's BASIC compiler BASCOM and IBM BASICA as QuickBASIC's direct ancestors. The current Pascal -> Delphi quote comes from Marco Cantu's Essential Pascal (secondary) and reads better as evidence for Turbo Pascal -> Delphi. Hejlsberg's 'C++ and Delphi also influenced our design' (Simple Talk, 2009) is a primary quote for Delphi -> C#. The Object Pascal Language Guide (Borland, 2002; https://azrael.digipen.edu/~mmead/www/Files/Borland/ObjectPascalLanguageGuide.pdf) was searched and contains no sentence relating Object Pascal to Turbo Pascal or Borland Pascal. Not reachable or not read: Computerworld A-Z C# interview (host not found), Turbo Pascal 4.0 Owner's Handbook and QuickBASIC 4.5 manual PDF (over the fetch size limit), Visual Studio Magazine Hejlsberg Q&A and classiccmp Whitten message (HTTP 403), the scanned original of the May 1991 Visual Basic press release (image only). The Turbo Pascal 3.0 manual file is a later reproduction of the 1985 manual ('This edition produced by ...'); the text is Borland's.
